        "content": "# @link-foundation/universal-translator\n\nTranslate programs between languages through a typed meta language, with\nmatching JavaScript and Rust implementations. The translator is built from\ngrammar and rule tables, not from per-program templates. It reads JavaScript,\nTypeScript, Python, Ruby, Lua, PHP, C, C++, C#, Java, Go, Rust, Kotlin,\nSwift, Perl, Dart, Scala, Julia, R, Groovy, Objective-C, Nim, D, Pascal,\nFortran, Ada, Visual Basic .NET, Bash, MATLAB/Octave, Zig, Lean 4 and Rocq\n(32 languages), and writes any of them. It can also lower a program to x86-64\nassembly (NASM), CIL (ILAsm) or JVM bytecode (Jasmin).\n\n## Translate a program\n\n```sh\nnpm ci\nnode bin/universal-translator.js translate javascript python examples/programs/factorial.js\nnode bin/universal-translator.js translate python rust - < program.py\nnode bin/universal-translator.js translate javascript nasm examples/programs/fizz-buzz.js\nnode bin/universal-translator.js meta go examples/programs/hand-written/sum-of-squares.go\nnode bin/universal-translator.js languages\ncargo run --locked -- translate-grammar javascript kotlin examples/programs/factorial.js\n```\n\nBoth CLIs read a file, or standard input when you omit the file or pass `-`.\nThe JavaScript package supports Node.js 20 and later, Bun and Deno.\n\nEach translation runs these stages:\n\n1. A lexer and a table-driven parser read the source language.\n2. Understanding rules turn the syntax tree into a meta program.\n3. Type inference gives every value a type.\n4. Meaning rules and any configured meta→meta layers rewrite the program.\n5. Context rules adapt it to the target language.\n6. An emitter writes the target syntax. For the machine targets, the program\n   is first lowered to a stack machine.\n\nPick a mode with `--mode`:\n\n- `context-dependent` (the default) adapts names, comments and terms such as\n  \"function\" or \"method\" to the target language.\n- `literal` keeps names and comment text as written.\n- `same-effect` keeps only what the program does and may restructure it.\n\nThe meta language has integers, text, booleans and integer arrays. Arrays\nare indexed from 0 in the meta language, and languages that count from 1\nshift every index. In C an array is a local variable-length array, so its\nlength is `sizeof a / sizeof a[0]`. The sieve, bubble sort and sum and\nproduct examples use arrays. The case study lists the other compromises.\n\n`createTranslator({ layers })` takes rule layers that can be replaced or\ndecorated. The common library in `common-library/` only hides differences\nbetween standard libraries, such as printing. `--common-library` translates\nevery print into a call to it.\n\nEvery program in `examples/programs` has been translated into every target\nin `examples/programs/translated`. These shared files are what the JavaScript\nand Rust tests check against. `node examples/programs/verify-native.mjs`\ncompiles and runs each translation with its native toolchain, and CI runs it\nwith `--require-all`.\n\n## Translate a statement or a function on its own\n\nA fragment is a whole program, one or more function definitions, or one or\nmore statements. `parseFragment` tries the source in that order and\nreturns its kind. `translateFragment` writes the same kind of fragment\nin the target, without a main function, a class or imports.\n\n```js\nimport {\n  parseFragment,\n  translateFragment,\n} from '@link-foundation/universal-translator';\n\nparseFragment('x = x + 1;', 'javascript').kind; // 'statements'\ntranslateFragment('x = x + 1;', 'javascript', 'pascal'); // 'x := x + 1;\\n'\ntranslateFragment('def square(n):\\n    return n * n\\n', 'python', 'rust');\n// 'fn square(n: i64) -> i64 {\\n    return n * n;\\n}\\n'\n```\n\n```sh\necho 'x = x + 1;' | node bin/universal-translator.js translate javascript pascal --fragment\n```\n\nThe Rust crate has `parse_fragment` and `translate_fragment`, as free\nfunctions and as methods of `Translator`, and its command line has the same\n`--fragment` flag. A fragment must be complete. A function ends with its\nclosing, a block statement with its end, and a single line statement is a\nwhole statement. Otherwise the error says what is missing and where, for\nexample `The fragment is not complete: it ends before its closing (line 2)`.\n\nEvery fragment in `examples/programs/fragments` is translated into every\nlanguage under `examples/programs/fragments/translated`. Both test suites\ncheck these files and read each of them back into the same JavaScript.\n\nLimits:\n\n- Variables that the fragment uses but does not declare stay undeclared.\n  Pascal, Fortran and Ada only declare the variables that the fragment\n  declares itself, and keep the spelling of the others as written. In Zig\n  such a variable is printed with `{any}`.\n- In Python, Ruby and other languages without declarations, `x = 5` is read\n  as a declaration.\n- In a natural language, a fragment is one or more sentences that match a\n  template of the language.\n- Machine targets (NASM, CIL, JVM) hold whole programs only. A statement or\n  function on its own is rejected.\n- Perl and Bash have no booleans, so `true` and `false` come back as 1 and 0.\n- Classes are not part of the meta language yet.\n\n## Translate to and from controlled natural languages\n\nControlled versions of 30 natural languages are languages like any other.\nThey are English, Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, French, Arabic, Bengali,\nPortuguese, Russian, Urdu, Indonesian, German, Japanese, Marathi, Telugu,\nTurkish, Tamil, Vietnamese, Korean, Italian, Persian, Swahili, Tagalog,\nThai, Polish, Ukrainian, Hausa, Gujarati, Punjabi and Dutch. Each one is\ndescribed as data in `data/natural/<id>.lino`: one sentence template for\nevery meta statement, one phrase for every operator, and a small lexicon\nfor program names. The writer and the reader use the same tables, so every\nsentence the writer produces is one the reader accepts.\n\n```sh\nnode bin/universal-translator.js translate javascript russian examples/programs/fizz-buzz.js\nnode bin/universal-translator.js translate english rust examples/programs/natural/factorial/factorial.english.txt\nnode bin/universal-translator.js translate nasm minimal-english examples/programs/translated/factorial/factorial.asm\nnode bin/universal-translator.js check-words english-e-prime examples/programs/natural/leap-year/leap-year.english-e-prime.txt\n```\n\n```text\nДля каждого число от 1 до 100 повторять это:\n  Если число по модулю 15 равно 0, сделать это:\n    Написать «FizzBuzz» и закончить строку.\n```\n\nProfiles extend a language and add the rules of a controlled language\nstandard. `checkText` and `check-words` enforce those rules:\n\n| Profile                   | Standard                                     | Rules that are checked                                |\n| ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |\n| `english` (`cnl-default`) | Balanced intersection of the standards below | One-to-one single-word lexicon; every text reads back |\n| `english-asd-ste100`      | ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English      | At most 20 words, imperative starts, word list        |\n| `english-ace`             | Attempto Controlled English                  | Sentences start with ACE's determiners and keywords   |\n| `english-gellish`         | Gellish Formal English                       | Templates use each listed Gellish relation phrase     |\n| `dutch-gellish`           | Gellish Formeel Nederlands                   | Templates use each listed Gellish relation phrase     |\n| `english-sbvr`            | SBVR Structured English                      | Sentences start with SBVR keywords                    |\n| `english-plain-language`  | Plain language (ISO 24495-1)                 | At most 25 words, 20 on average; no \"shall\"           |\n| `english-e-prime`         | E-Prime                                      | No form of \"to be\"                                    |\n| `english-basic-english`   | Basic English (Ogden's 850 words)            | At most 25 words; template words from Ogden's list    |\n| `english-special-english` | VOA Special English / Learning English       | Template words from its word list, short sentences    |\n| `english-globish`         | Globish                                      | At most 20 words; template words from Globish list    |\n| `minimal-english`         | Minimal English (NSM)                        | Template words are semantic primes or molecules       |\n| `minimal-french`          | Minimal French (NSM)                         | Template words are semantic primes or molecules       |\n| `minimal-polish`          | Minimal Polish (NSM)                         | Template words are semantic primes or molecules       |\n\nThe 65 semantic primes of Natural Semantic Metalanguage are listed in\n`data/natural/semantic-primes.lino` with their English, French, Polish,\nRussian and Spanish exponents. Every example program is written in every\nlanguage and profile in `examples/programs/natural`. The tests read each\ntext back to the same meaning, check it against the rules of its standard\nand translate it to every programming language. The Rust implementation\n(`rust/src/natural/`) reads the same data, writes the same texts byte for\nbyte and has the same `languages` and `check-words` commands.\n\n`node scripts/check-requirements.mjs` checks every requirement of issue 1\nagainst `docs/case-studies/issue-1/requirements.lino`, and CI fails while any\nof them is neither done nor reported as blocked.\n\nSee the [runnable examples](examples/translation/README.md) and the\n[issue 1 case study](docs/case-studies/issue-1/README.md).\n\n## Library, CLI, HTTP API and Docker\n\nThe same translator is available four ways:\n\n```js\nimport {\n  createTranslator,\n  createTranslationServer,\n} from '@link-foundation/universal-translator';\n\ncreateTranslator().translate('console.log(\"Hi\");', 'javascript', 'python');\ncreateTranslationServer().listen(8080); // GET /languages, POST /translate\n```\n\n```bash\nuniversal-translator translate javascript python app.js\nuniversal-translator serve --port 8080   # or PORT=8080, or PORT: 8080 in .lenv\ncurl -d '{\"source\":\"console.log(\\\"Hi\\\");\",\"from\":\"javascript\",\"to\":\"rust\"}' \\\n  -H 'content-type: application/json' http://localhost:8080/translate\ndocker build -t universal-translator .\ndocker run --rm -p 8080:8080 universal-translator          # the HTTP API\ndocker run --rm -i universal-translator translate javascript go - < app.js\n```\n\n`POST /translate` takes `{source, from, to, fragment?, mode?, commonLibrary?,\nallOrNothing?, rules?}` and answers `{output, complete, errors, coverage?,\ndetected?}`, or `{error}` with status 400. Regular expression rules are refused unless the\nserver is created with `createTranslationServer({ allowRegexRules: true })`.\n\n### Partial translation, detection and The Rust implementation\n(`rust/src/natural/`) reads the same data, writes the same texts byte for\nbyte and has the same `languages` and `check-words` commands.\n\n`node scripts/check-requirements.mjs` checks every requirement of issue 1\nagainst `docs/case-studies/issue-1/requirements.lino`, and CI fails while any\nof them is neither done nor reported as blocked.\n\nSee the [runnable examples](examples/translation/README.md) and the\n[issue 1 case study](docs/case-studies/issue-1/README.md).\n\n## Library, CLI, HTTP API and Docker\n\nThe same translator is available four ways:\n\n```js\nimport {\n  createTranslator,\n  createTranslationServer,\n} from '@link-foundation/universal-translator';\n\ncreateTranslator().translate('console.log(\"Hi\");', 'javascript', 'python');\ncreateTranslationServer().listen(8080); // GET /languages, POST /translate\n```\n\n```bash\nuniversal-translator translate javascript python app.js\nuniversal-translator serve --port 8080   # or PORT=8080, or PORT: 8080 in .lenv\ncurl -d '{\"source\":\"console.log(\\\"Hi\\\");\",\"from\":\"javascript\",\"to\":\"rust\"}' \\\n  -H 'content-type: application/json' http://localhost:8080/translate\ndocker build -t universal-translator .\ndocker run --rm -p 8080:8080 universal-translator          # the HTTP API\ndocker run --rm -i universal-translator translate javascript go - < app.js\n```\n\n`POST /translate` takes `{source, from, to, fragment?, mode?, commonLibrary?,\nallOrNothing?, rules?}` and answers `{output, complete, errors, coverage?,\ndetected?}`, or `{error}` with status 400. Regular expression rules are refused unless the\nserver is created with `createTranslationServer({ allowRegexRules: true })`.\n\n### Partial translation, detection and         "content": "### Partial translation, detection and rules\n\nTranslation is partial by default. Whatever reads is translated, and every\npart that does not is kept as a comment with its error:\n\n```bash\nuniversal-translator translate auto javascript app.py   # detect the source\nuniversal-translator translate python go app.py --all-or-nothing\nuniversal-translator coverage python app.py   # lines:, readLines:, coverage:, errors:, parts:\nuniversal-translator detect app.py            # the likeliest languages first, one per line\nuniversal-translator detect app.py --json     # either report as JSON\nuniversal-translator translate russian python a.txt --rules examples/rules/russian-at-most.lino\n```\n\n```js\nimport {\n  createTranslator,\n  detectLanguage,\n  translatePartial,\n} from '@link-foundation/universal-translator';\n\ntranslatePartial(\n  'x = 1\\nwith open(f) as g:\\n    y = 2\\n',\n  'python',\n  'javascript'\n);\n// { text, complete: false, errors: [{ line: 2, endLine: 2, message }], coverage }\ndetectLanguage('fn main() {}\\n')[0].id; // 'rust'\n\n// Rules as data, one list per stage of the pipeline:\ncreateTranslator({\n  rules: {\n    source: [{ find: 'ничего', replace: 'Ничего', language: 'russian' }],\n    templates: {\n      russian: { 'less-or-equal': ['{left} самое большее {right}'] },\n    },\n    names: [{ find: 'n', replace: 'count' }],\n    output: [{ find: '(\\\\d+)', replace: '[$1]', regex: true }],\n  },\n});\n```\n\nA rule file is indented Links Notation. A stage, a natural language and a\ntemplate key are unique, so each is written as `name:`. The rules of a\nstage are a list with one rule per line, each made of a few `(field value)`\nlinks. `readRules` and `formatRules` (Rust: `custom_rules::read_rules` and\n`format_rules`) turn the text into the object above and back, and JSON rule\nfiles are still read. This is\n[examples/rules/russian-at-most.lino](examples/rules/russian-at-most.lino):\n\n```\nsource:\n  (find ничего) (replace Ничего) (language russian)\ntemplates:\n  russian:\n    less-or-equal: '{left} самое большее {right}'\nnames:\n  (find n) (replace count)\noutput:\n  (find pass) (replace 'pass  # ничего') (language python)\n  (find '(\\d+)') (replace '[$1]') (regex true) (language javascript)\n```\n\n`POST /translate` takes `rules` as this text or as the object.\n\n### Language versions, comment languages and the meta view\n\nA target may name a version of a language (`python@2`, `english-british`,\n`minimal-russian`). Comments are kept with their spacing, as in a concrete\nsyntax tree, and may be translated to another natural language on their\nown. When `--comment-from` is left out, the comment language is detected:\n\n```bash\nuniversal-translator translate javascript python@2 app.js --comment-language russian\nuniversal-translator translate python python app.py --comment-language german  # comments only\nuniversal-translator meta python app.py   # the meta language as an indented tree\nuniversal-translator meta python app.py --json   # the same program as JSON\n```\n\nThe meta view is indented Links Notation: one line per node with its kind,\nits main value and its other plain fields as `(name value)` links, and its\nchild nodes nested below it with no field labels and no block markers. A\nfield that follows a block, such as the `else` branch, is introduced by one\nplain word (`otherwise`):\n\n```\nprogram\n  function twice (blank-after true) (return-type integer)\n    parameter n (type integer)\n    if\n      binary greater (type boolean)\n        name n (type integer)\n        number 1 (type integer)\n      return\n        binary multiply (type integer)\n          name n (type integer)\n          number 2 (type integer)\n      otherwise\n        return\n          number 0 (type integer)\n```\n\n```js\nimport {\n  createTranslator,\n  formatMeta,\n  translateComments,\n  versionsOf,\n  naturalLanguageVersions,\n} from '@link-foundation/universal-translator';\n\nconst translator = createTranslator();\ntranslator.translate('// number\\nlet x = 1;\\n', 'javascript', 'python@2', {\n  commentLanguage: 'russian',\n}); // '# число\\nx = 1\\n'\ntranslateComments('# number\\nx = 1\\n', 'python', { to: 'russian' });\nformatMeta(translator.toMeta('x = 1\\n', 'python'));\nversionsOf('python'); // [{ version: '3', default: true }, { version: '2' }]\nnaturalLanguageVersions('english'); // regions, standards and minimal-english\n```\n\nEvery natural language has a `minimal-<id>` version restricted to the 65\nsemantic primes of Natural Semantic Metalanguage. `createStandard`,\n`defineWord` and `wikidataLookup` build a standard of at most 1024 words\nwhose other words are defined recursively through it. GOFAI): its knowledge is an inspectable [semantic network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semantic_network) of human-readable links rather than hidden neural weights. The [associative technology stack guide](docs/associative-tech-stack.md) links every component and distinguishes direct runtime dependencies from architecture and development tooling. The case study in [docs/case-studies/issue-451](docs/case-studies/issue-451/README.md) maps the field's best practices onto this associative stack; the design study in [docs/case-studies/issue-649](docs/case-studies/issue-649/README.md) audits how the same stack expresses symbolic **world models** — a current-state and target-state context, their difference, context merge/split, and predicting the consequences of an action, all as links networks rather than embeddings; and the study in [docs/case-studies/issue-686](docs/case-studies/issue-686/README.md) adds **usage-weighted persistence** of meta-language expressions — counting reads and writes and incoming/outgoing link degree so the most used, most changed, and most connected knowledge persists longest, all as a links network.\n\nThe current implementation covers the surface area requested in issue #1:\n\n- library API for symbolic prompt handling\n- CLI chat command\n- HTTP API server with protocol namespaces under `/api/openai/v1`,\n  `/api/anthropic/v1`, `/api/gemini/v1beta`, and `/api/vertex/v1`\n- Telegram bot CLI with long polling by default and an opt-in webhook server, configured through statements.\thttps://github.com/link-foundation/relative-meta-logic\tThe Unlicense\tRust\t2026-11-21T20:07:55Z\n# relative-meta-logic\n\nA prototype for logic framework that can reason about anything relative to given probability of input statements.\n\n> **Note on naming:** This project was previously called *Associative-Dependent Logic (ADL)*. The name *Associative Dependent Meta Logic* is also valid, as in [dependent types](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dependent_type), but *relative* is closer to the concept of a [link](https://github.com/link-foundation/meta-theory), and actually all statements are relative to other statements. The name *meta-logic* reflects that this system can reason about all possible logic systems, including itself.\n\n## Implementations\n\nThis project provides two equivalent implementations:\n\n- **[JavaScript](./js/)** — Node.js implementation using the official [links-notation](https://github.com/link-foundation/links-notation) parser\n- **[Rust](./rust/)** — Rust implementation using the official [links-notation](https://github.com/link-foundation/links-notation) crate\n\nBoth implementations pass the same comprehensive test suites and produce identical results.\n\nFor implementation details, see [ARCHITECTURE.md](./ARCHITECTURE.md).\nFor versioning, deprecations, and release expectations, see\n[Compatibility and release policy](./docs/COMPATIBILITY.md).\n\n## Comparisons\n\n- [Core concept comparison](./docs/CONCEPTS-COMPARISON.md) - RML vs Twelf, LF, HELF, Isabelle, Coq/Rocq, Lean, Foundation, AFP, Abella, lambda Prolog, and Pecan by logical/metatheoretic concepts.\n- [Product feature comparison](./docs/FEATURE-COMPARISON.md) - RML vs the same systems by authoring workflow, automation, libraries, tooling, and distribution.\n- [Configurability and operator redefinition](./docs/CONFIGURABILITY.md) - Why every operator, truth constant, range, and valence is redefinable at runtime, with the precedence rules and a comparison to Lean/Rocq fixed semantics.\n- [Foundations and root-construct registry](./docs/FOUNDATIONS.md) - The trust catalogue of every primitive the kernel depends on, the `(foundation …)` / `(with-foundation …)` / `(foundation-report)` surface, the bundled Boolean and Kleene foundations, and the backward-compatibility guarantee.\n- [Typed kernel rules](./docs/KERNEL.md) - The implemented D1 rules for `Pi`, `lambda`, `apply`, `(expr of Type)`, and `(type of expr)`.\n- [Soundness statement](./docs/SOUNDNESS.md) - The trusted-kernel guarantee, proof-replay checker, trusted operator base, and aggregator-relative scope of soundness.\n- [Metatheorem checker](./docs/METATHEOREMS.md) - The C3 Twelf-style guarantee that composes D12 totality, D14 coverage, D15 modes, and D13 termination, plus the `rml-meta` CLI.\n- [Lean 4 export](./docs/LEAN_EXPORT.md) - The `rml export lean` bridge for typed, non-probabilistic RML fragments.\n- [Rocq export](./docs/ROCQ-EXPORT.md) - The supported typed LiNo subset for `rml export rocq <file.lino> -o <file.v>`.\n- [Language Server](./docs/LANGUAGE_SERVER.md) - Stdio LSP setup for diagnostics, hover, go-to-definition, and completion in Neovim and Helix.\n\n## Tutorials\n\n- [Tutorial path](./docs/tutorials/) - The supported SHA-1 profile keeps exact UTF-8 commit\ntext, every complete ordered tree on the original path, modes, object identities\nand original blob bytes. Verification recomputes each object identity against\nthe independently supplied original revision and path, with explicit resource\nbounds. Normal verification needs neither the Git database nor a network read;\nautomatic capture reads the original objects. Unsupported encodings and formats\nrefuse. This establishes immutable source membership, not semantic equivalence\nbetween concepts. The original loan receipt uses this path without changing its\nsource revision, expected contents or predecessor assertions. The object framing\nfollows the [Git object model](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Internals-Git-Objects).\n\n## One common language of links\n\nMeta-language provides **one common, extensible language, represented\nrecursively as links and serialized in Links Notation**. It covers:\n\n- language grammars and the concepts they define;\n- complete concrete syntax trees, produced by default;\n- optional abstract syntax trees that keep explicit provenance back to the\n  concrete syntax;\n- semantic representations: bindings, types, universes, effects, ownership,\n  macros and notation, and proofs;\n- the transformations and translations over all of the above.\n\nA grammar, a parsed document, a semantic annotation and a transformation rule are\nall links in one network. None of them lives in a side table, an opaque string\npayload or a host-language callback that the network cannot inspect.\n\nThe goal is coverage of **all existing languages**. The popular languages,\ndialects, grammar formats and downstream workloads named here and in the ledger\nare mandatory minimum inventories, not a permanent shortlist.\n\nBoth runtime packages, the Rust crate `meta-language` and the npm package\n`meta-language`, implement the same features with the same observable behavior.\n[`parity/language-features.lino`](../parity/language-features.lino) enforces\nthis, and the runtime-parity rows of the ledger check it again on shared\nfixtures.\n\n### Global concept space\n\nAll grammars of all languages inhabit **one global concept space**. It supports [many-valued logics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Many-valued_logic) from unary (1-valued) through continuous probabilistic ([fuzzy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuzzy_logic)), allowing you to:\n\n- Define terms\n- Assign probabilities (truth values) to logical expressions\n- Redefine logical operators with different semantics\n- Configure truth value ranges: `[0, 1]` or `[-1, 1]` (balanced/symmetric)\n- Configure logic valence: 2-valued ([Boolean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra)), 3-valued ([ternary/Kleene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-valued_logic)), N-valued, or continuous\n- Use and redefine truth constants: `true`, `false`, `unknown`, `undefined`\n- Use and redefine Belnap operators: `both...and` (contradiction/avg) and `neither...nor` (gap/product)\n- Resolve paradoxical statements (e.g. the [liar paradox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liar_paradox))\n- Perform decimal-precision arithmetic (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`) — `0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3`, not `0.30000000000000004`\n- Query the truth value of complex expressions\n- Define dependent types as links — universe hierarchy, Pi-types, lambdas, type queries\n- Combine types with probabilistic logic in a unified framework\n- Delegate domain-specific decision blocks through evaluator plugins, including\n  `(domain automatic-sequences (theorem thue-morse-cube-free))`\n- Reuse the evaluator as a library, including a meta-expression adapter that accepts selected interpretations and explicit dependencies while keeping underspecified claims partial\n- Export the simply typed LiNo fragment to Isabelle/HOL source for external certification experiments\n\n## Supported Logic https://authoring-docs-microsoft.poolparty.biz/devrel/8b896464-3b7d-4e1f-84b0-9bb45aeb5f64\nspProducts:\n- https://authoring-docs-microsoft.poolparty.biz/devrel/69c76c32-967e-4c65-b89a-74cc527db725\n- https://microsoft-devrel.poolparty.biz/DevRelOfferingOntology/3f56b378-07a9-4fa1-afe8-9889fdc77628\n- https://authoring-docs-microsoft.poolparty.biz/devrel/b1d2d671-9549-46e8-918c-24349120dbf5\nplatformId: 1533e402-73c7-dd52-bc76-92014d329dc1\n---\n\n# Use the .NET Compiler Platform SDK syntax model - C# | Microsoft Learn\n\nThe *syntax tree* is a fundamental immutable data structure exposed by the compiler APIs. These trees represent the lexical and syntactic structure of source code. They serve two important purposes:\r\n\r\n- To allow tools - such as an IDE, add-ins, code analysis tools, and refactorings - to see and process the syntactic structure of source code in a user's project.\r\n- To enable tools - such as refactorings and an IDE - to create, modify, and rearrange source code in a natural manner without having to use direct text edits. By creating and manipulating trees, tools can easily create and rearrange source code.\r\n\r\n## Syntax trees\r\n\r\nSyntax trees are the primary structure used for compilation, code analysis, binding, refactoring, IDE features, and code generation. No part of the source code is understood without it first being identified and categorized into one of many well-known structural language elements.\r\n\r\nNote\r\n\r\n[RoslynQuoter](https://github.com/KirillOsenkov/RoslynQuoter) is an open-source tool that shows the syntax factory API calls used to construct a program's syntax tree. To try it out live, see [http://roslynquoter.azurewebsites.net](https://roslynquoter.azurewebsites.net).\r\n\r\nSyntax trees have three key attributes:\r\n\r\n- They hold all the source information in full fidelity. Full fidelity means that the syntax tree contains every piece of information found in the source text, every grammatical construct, every lexical token, and everything else in between, including white space, comments, and preprocessor directives. For example, each literal mentioned in the source is represented exactly as it was typed. Syntax trees also capture errors in source code when the program is incomplete or malformed by representing skipped or missing tokens.\r\n- They can produce the exact text that they were parsed from. From any syntax node, it's possible to get the text representation of the subtree rooted at that node. This ability means that syntax trees can be used as a way to construct and edit source text. By creating a tree you have, by implication, created the equivalent text, and by making a new tree out of changes to an existing tree, you have effectively edited the text.\r\n- They are immutable and thread-safe. After a tree is obtained, it's a snapshot of the current state of the code and never changes. This allows multiple users to interact with the same syntax tree at the same time in different threads without locking or duplication. Because the trees are immutable and no modifications can be made directly to a tree, factory methods help create and modify syntax trees by creating additional snapshots of the tree. The trees are efficient in the way they reuse underlying nodes, so a new version can be rebuilt fast and with little extra memory.\r\n\r\nA syntax tree is literally a tree data structure, where non-terminal structural elements parent other elements. Each syntax tree is made up of nodes, tokens, and trivia.\r\n\r\n## Syntax nodes\r\n\r\nSyntax nodes are one of the primary elements of syntax trees. These nodes represent syntactic constructs such as declarations, statements, clauses, and expressions. Each category of syntax nodes is represented by a separate class derived from [Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.SyntaxNode](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxnode). The set of node classes is not extensible.\r\n\r\nAll syntax nodes are non-terminal nodes in the syntax tree, which means they always have other nodes and tokens as children. As a child of another node, each node has a parent node that can be accessed through the [SyntaxNode.Parent](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxnode.parent#microsoft-codeanalysis-syntaxnode-parent) property. Because nodes and trees are immutable, the parent of a node never changes. The root of the tree has a null parent.\r\n\r\nEach node has a [SyntaxNode.ChildNodes()](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxnode.childnodes#microsoft-codeanalysis-syntaxnode-childnodes) method, which returns a list of child nodes in sequential order based on their position in the source text. This list does not contain tokens. Each node also has methods to examine Descendants, such as [DescendantNodes](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxnode.descendantnodes), [DescendantTokens](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxnode.descendanttokens), or [DescendantTrivia](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxnode.descendanttrivia) - that represent a list of all the nodes, tokens, or trivia that exist in the subtree rooted by that node.\r\n\r\nIn addition, each syntax node subclass exposes all the same children through strongly typed properties. For example, a [BinaryExpressionSyntax](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharp.syntax.binaryexpressionsyntax) node class has three additional properties specific to binary operators: [Left](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharp.syntax.binaryexpressionsyntax.left#microsoft-codeanalysis-csharp-syntax-binaryexpressionsyntax-left), [OperatorToken](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharp.syntax.binaryexpressionsyntax.operatortoken#microsoft-codeanalysis-csharp-syntax-binaryexpressionsyntax-operatortoken), and [Right](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharp.syntax.binaryexpressionsyntax.right#microsoft-codeanalysis-csharp-syntax-binaryexpressionsyntax-right). The type of [Left](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharp.syntax.binaryexpressionsyntax.left#microsoft-codeanalysis-csharp-syntax-binaryexpressionsyntax-left) and [Right](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharp.syntax.binaryexpressionsyntax.right#microsoft-codeanalysis-csharp-syntax-binaryexpressionsyntax-right) is [ExpressionSyntax](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharp.syntax.expressionsyntax), and the type of [OperatorToken](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharp.syntax.binaryexpressionsyntax.operatortoken#microsoft-codeanalysis-csharp-syntax-binaryexpressionsyntax-operatortoken) is [SyntaxToken](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxtoken).\r\n\r\nSome syntax nodes have optional children. For example, an [IfStatementSyntax](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharp.syntax.ifstatementsyntax) has an optional [ElseClauseSyntax](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharp.syntax.elseclausesyntax). If the child is not present, the property returns null.\r\n\r\n## Syntax tokens\r\n\r\nSyntax tokens are the terminals of the language grammar, representing the smallest syntactic fragments of the code. They are never parents of other nodes or tokens. Syntax tokens consist of keywords, identifiers, literals, and punctuation.\r\n\r\nFor efficiency purposes, the [SyntaxToken](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxtoken) type is a CLR value type. Therefore, unlike syntax nodes, there is only one structure for all kinds of tokens with a mix of properties that have meaning depending on the kind of token that is being represented.\r\n\r\nFor example, an integer literal token represents a numeric value. In addition to the raw source text the token spans, the literal token has a [Value](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxtoken.value#microsoft-codeanalysis-syntaxtoken-value) property that tells you the exact decoded integer value. This property is typed as [Object](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.object) because it may be one of many primitive types.\r\n\r\nThe [ValueText](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxtoken.valuetext#microsoft-codeanalysis-syntaxtoken-valuetext) property tells you the same information as the [Value](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxtoken.value#microsoft-codeanalysis-syntaxtoken-value) property; however this property is always typed as [String](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.string). An identifier in C# source text may include Unicode escape characters, yet the syntax of the escape sequence itself is not considered part of the identifier name. So although the raw text spanned by the token does include the escape sequence, the [ValueText](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxtoken.valuetext#microsoft-codeanalysis-syntaxtoken-valuetext) property does not. Instead, it includes the Unicode characters identified by the escape. For example, if the source text contains an identifier written as `\\u03C0`, then the [ValueText](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxtoken.valuetext#microsoft-codeanalysis-syntaxtoken-valuetext) property for this token will return `π`.\r\n\r\n## Syntax trivia\r\n\r\nSyntax trivia represent the parts of the source text that are largely insignificant for normal understanding of the code, such as white space, comments, and preprocessor directives. Like syntax tokens, trivia are value types. The single [Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.SyntaxTrivia](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxtrivia) type is used to describe all kinds of trivia.\r\n\r\nBecause trivia are not part of the normal language syntax and can appear anywhere between any two tokens, they are not included in the syntax tree as a child of a node. Yet, because they are important when implementing a feature like refactoring and to maintain full fidelity with the source text, they do exist as part of the syntax tree.\r\n\r\nYou can access trivia by inspecting a token's [SyntaxToken.LeadingTrivia](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxtoken.leadingtrivia#microsoft-codeanalysis-syntaxtoken-leadingtrivia) or [SyntaxToken.TrailingTrivia](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxtoken.trailingtrivia#microsoft-codeanalysis-syntaxtoken-trailingtrivia) collections. When source text is parsed, sequences of trivia are associated with tokens. In general, a token owns any trivia after it on the same line up to the next token. Any trivia after that line is associated with the following token. The first token in the source file gets all the initial trivia, and the last sequence of trivia in the file is tacked onto the end-of-file token, which otherwise has zero width.\r\n\r\nUnlike syntax nodes and tokens, syntax trivia do not have parents. Yet, because they are part of the tree and each is associated with a single token, you may access the token it is associated with using the [SyntaxTrivia.Token](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxtrivia.token#microsoft-codeanalysis-syntaxtrivia-token) property.\r\n\r\n## Spans\r\n\r\nEach node, token, or trivia knows its position within the source text and the number of characters it consists of. A text position is represented as a 32-bit integer, which is a zero-based `char` index. A [TextSpan](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.text.textspan) object is the beginning position and a count of characters, both represented as integers. If [TextSpan](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.text.textspan) has a zero length, it refers to a location between two characters.\r\n\r\nEach node has two [TextSpan](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.text.textspan) properties: [Span](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxnode.span) and [FullSpan](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxnode.fullspan).\r\n\r\nThe [Span](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxnode.span#microsoft-codeanalysis-syntaxnode-span) property is the text span from the start of the first token in the node's subtree to the end of the last token. This span does not include any leading or trailing trivia.\r\n\r\nThe [FullSpan](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxnode.fullspan#microsoft-codeanalysis-syntaxnode-fullspan) property is the text span that includes the node's normal span, plus the span of any leading or trailing trivia.\r\n\r\nFor example:\r\n\r\n```csharp\r\n      if (x > 3)\r\n      {\r\n||        // this is bad\r\n          |throw new Exception(\"Not right.\");|  // better exception?||\r\n      }\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe statement node inside the block has a span indicated by the single vertical bars (|). It includes the characters `throw new Exception(\"Not right.\");`. The full span is indicated by the double vertical bars (||). It includes the same characters as the span and the characters associated with the leading and trailing trivia.\r\n\r\n## Kinds\r\n\r\nEach node, token, or trivia has a [SyntaxNode.RawKind](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxnode.rawkind#microsoft-codeanalysis-syntaxnode-rawkind) property, of type [System.Int32](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.int32), that identifies the exact syntax element represented. This value can be cast to a language-specific enumeration. Each language, C# or Visual Basic, has a single `SyntaxKind` enumeration ([Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp.SyntaxKind](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharp.syntaxkind) and [Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.VisualBasic.SyntaxKind](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.visualbasic.syntaxkind), respectively) that lists all the possible nodes, tokens, and trivia elements in the grammar. This conversion can be done automatically by accessing the [CSharpExtensions.Kind](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharp.csharpextensions.kind) or [VisualBasicExtensions.Kind](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.visualbasic.visualbasicextensions.kind) extension methods.\r\n\r\nThe [RawKind](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxtoken.rawkind#microsoft-codeanalysis-syntaxtoken-rawkind) property allows for easy disambiguation of syntax node types that share the same node class. For tokens and trivia, this property is the only way to distinguish one type of element from another.\r\n\r\nFor example, a single [BinaryExpressionSyntax](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharp.syntax.binaryexpressionsyntax) class has [Left](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharp.syntax.binaryexpressionsyntax.left#microsoft-codeanalysis-csharp-syntax-binaryexpressionsyntax-left), [OperatorToken](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharp.syntax.binaryexpressionsyntax.operatortoken#microsoft-codeanalysis-csharp-syntax-binaryexpressionsyntax-operatortoken), and [Right](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharp.syntax.binaryexpressionsyntax.right#microsoft-codeanalysis-csharp-syntax-binaryexpressionsyntax-right) as children. The [Kind](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharp.csharpextensions.kind) method distinguishes whether it's an [AddExpression](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharp.syntaxkind#microsoft-codeanalysis-csharp-syntaxkind-addexpression), [SubtractExpression](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharp.syntaxkind#microsoft-codeanalysis-csharp-syntaxkind-subtractexpression), or [MultiplyExpression](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharp.syntaxkind#microsoft-codeanalysis-csharp-syntaxkind-multiplyexpression) kind of syntax node.\r\n\r\nTip\r\n\r\nIt's recommended to check kinds using [IsKind](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharpextensions.iskind) (for C#) or [IsKind](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.visualbasicextensions.iskind) (for VB) extension methods.\r\n\r\n## Errors\r\n\r\nEven when the source text contains syntax errors, a full syntax tree that is round-trippable to the source is exposed. When the parser encounters code that does not conform to the defined syntax of the language, it uses one of two techniques to create a syntax tree:\r\n\r\n- If the parser expects a particular kind of token but does not find it, it may insert a missing token into the syntax tree in the location that the token was expected. A missing token represents the actual token that was expected, but it has an empty span, and its [SyntaxNode.IsMissing](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.syntaxnode.ismissing#microsoft-codeanalysis-syntaxnode-ismissing) property returns `true`.\r\n- The parser may skip tokens until it finds one where it can continue parsing. In this case, the skipped tokens are attached as a trivia node with the kind [SkippedTokensTrivia](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.csharp.syntaxkind#microsoft-codeanalysis-csharp-syntaxkind-skippedtokenstrivia)."
      }

The parser itself never sees whitespace; the `TreeSink` layer attaches it to the tree, and comments are attached heuristically. Each token stores its full text, so concatenating all token texts in order reproduces the original file. The guide also describes alternatives, such as separating trivia into leading and trailing lists (Swift, Roslyn) or using explicit trivia nodes (IntelliJ, rowan).\n\n- **Green and red trees:** The green tree is an immutable, untyped structure that stores each node's kind and text length, with text held at the leaves. Interning lets identical tokens and subtrees share memory. The red layer, `SyntaxNode`, is a cursor over the green tree that adds parent links, absolute text offsets, and identity-based equality. Only the green tree stores data; the red layer is a view onto it.\n\n- **Error resilience:** Parser errors are kept out of the tree and collected separately. Unexpected input is wrapped in an `ERROR` node and treated like any other node. A missing grammar-required node is simply absent. The guide states that parsing stays lossless even for invalid input, and the parser continues past errors to recover as much structure as it can.\n\n- **Typed AST over the untyped tree:** The AST layer consists of thin wrappers around `SyntaxNode` that perform checked casts. Around 117 concrete node types are generated, with enums for variant families and traits for shared substructures. All accessors are optional so incomplete code can be represented, and any AST node can be turned back into an untyped `SyntaxNode`."

The config's `theme` maps each name to a color.\n\nLocal variable queries (`locals.scm`) use fixed captures: `@local.scope`, `@local.definition`, and `@local.reference`. The `@ignore` capture excludes nodes from tagging. Highlight patterns can use `(#is-not? local)` to skip identifiers identified as local variables, so references and their definitions are colored consistently."

The toolchains include Lean 4 (elan), Rocq (opam), fpc, gnat, gfortran, octave, zig, nim, ldc, Objective-C, Swift, Kotlin, Scala, .NET and Jasmin.\n- **`experiments/verify-syntax-exchange.sh`.** The JS and Rust command lines list the same 32 languages and write identical output.\n- **`node scripts/check-requirements.mjs`.** The requirements gate described above.\n- **`npm run test:coverage`.** The coverage gate described above.\n- **`web-e2e`.** The browser test of the demo.\n- **`--trace`.** Logs each pipeline stage.\n\n### CI reliability (native translation job)\n\n- Toolchain archives are cached. Each download attempt is capped at 3 minutes and falls back to a mirror: Google's Maven Central mirror for Groovy and `zig.linus.dev` for Zig, all checked by SHA-256. This fixes a run where the step hung on a stalled download.\n- `verify-native.mjs` runs its checks in parallel worker processes.\n- `js/tests/ci-timeouts.test.js` keeps each job's step budgets within 70% of its backstop.\n=======7\n| Comment language apart from the code language | `commentLanguage` option, CLI flag and demo picker. The same code can be kept with only its comments translated | `comments.test.js`, e2e |\n| Edge cases and symmetry across all languages | Every vocabulary word of every language takes effect when changed. Empty-line fidelity is checked for every language in both directions. Fixed: Perl and Bash read `return 1` back as `true`; a comment above `#include` was dropped; a CodeQL prototype-pollution alert; the server test hung under Deno because Deno's `server.close()` waits for kept-alive fetch connections (`experiments/deno-server-close.mjs`) | `vocabulary-effect.test.js`, `comments.test.js`, `rust/tests/grammar.rs` |\n| Edit every standard in a separate tab and save one's own | Standards tab: every word and the meta language concept it stands for. The issue 8 requirements are now checked by the same gate | `issue-6-with-8.test.js`, `rust/tests/issue_6.rs`, `universal-app.test.js`, e2e, gate entries `with-partial-translation` and `docs/case-studies/issue-8/requirements.lino` |\n| Same features in the Rust crate | Language versions (`python@2`), natural language versions, comment languages, comment language detection and `--comment-language`/`--comment-from` in `rust/`, with the same outputs as JS. When standard input isn't ready yet, `readFileSync(0)` throws `EAGAIN` (for example `(sleep 1; echo 'print(1)') | universal-translator translate python javascript -`), and a reader that closes early (`| head`) caused an unhandled `EPIPE`. Now `readStandardInput` waits through `EAGAIN`, and `EPIPE` ends the CLI quietly. The test `js/tests/cli-pipes.test.js` uses real shell pipes; it fails before the fix and passes after.\n- **P9**: `coverage` and `detect` printed JSON by default, against requirement 8. They now print indented Links Notation in both CLIs; `--json` still prints JSON.\n\nNot done in this PR. Only modified nodes are reprinted. If a modified node can't be reprinted from the original source, Recast falls back to a generic pretty printer, so the worst case is some reformatting. The README guarantees that printing an unmodified parse returns the source exactly: `\"recast.print(recast.parse(source)).code === source\"`.\n\n**API:**\n- `parse(source, options)`: returns the AST. It uses Esprima by default, and the `parser` option can supply others, such as Babel or TypeScript.\n- `print(ast, options)`: reprints only the changed parts and returns `{ code, map }`, with an optional source map.\n- `prettyPrint(ast, options)`: fully reformats the code and discards the original formatting."

        "type": "tool_result",
        "content": "**LibCST** is a Python syntax tree library that combines the strengths of an AST and a concrete syntax tree (CST).\n\n- **CST vs. AST:** An AST keeps a program's meaning but drops comments and formatting, so the original source can't be rebuilt from it. A traditional CST, like lib2to3's, keeps everything but mirrors Python's grammar, which makes semantic edits awkward. LibCST is lossless and its node types and fields are organized to match Python's semantics.\n\n- **Whitespace nodes:** Instead of storing whitespace in `prefix` strings, LibCST parses it into explicit nodes such as `SimpleWhitespace`, `TrailingWhitespace`, and `Comma`. Each node owns its own spacing, so removing a function argument doesn't require manually fixing stray commas.\n\n- **Round trip:** Because whitespace and comments are retained, parsing code and reprinting it yields the exact original source, and this still holds after the tree is modified.\n\n- **Whitespace attachment:** Blank lines and comments above a statement go in `leading_lines`. A line's trailing spaces, comment, and newline go in `trailing_whitespace`. Spacing inside expressions is stored on the relevant node, such as `whitespace_before_args` on a `Call` or `whitespace_after_arg` on an `Arg`. Module-level details like `default_indent`, `default_newline`, and `has_trailing_newline` are stored on `Module`.\n\n- **Codegen:** Generating code from the tree reproduces the source text, including each node's whitespace, so unmodified parts come out unchanged.\n\nThe trade-offs are slower parsing and more complex implementations for tools that focus mainly on whitespace."

One grammar can parse text, generate text, and translate between languages.\n\n- **Abstract syntax** (`abstract`) defines the meanings a grammar can express. `cat` declares categories (types of meaning), and `fun` declares functions that build syntax trees from them.\n- **Concrete syntax** (`concrete ... of Abstract`) maps those meanings to strings, one concrete syntax per language. `lincat` gives each category a linearization type, usually a record with a string field `s`. `lin` gives each function its string-building rule.\n- **Linearization** turns a tree into a string.\n- **Parsing** turns a string into a tree, and fails if the grammar does not cover it.\n- **Translation** parses a sentence in one language and linearizes the resulting tree in another. Without a language flag, linearization produces all available languages.\n- **Resource grammar library** provides ready-made syntax and morphology for many languages, so you can build phrases from categories like noun phrase and clause without handling inflection yourself.\n- **Functors and interfaces** let you write a shared concrete syntax once against an interface. Each language then supplies a small lexicon instance and a short instantiation.\n\n**Example** (a minimal grammar of my own):\n\n```\nabstract Shop = {\n  flags startcat = Phrase ;\n  cat Phrase ; Item ;\n  fun Want : Item -> Phrase ;\n      Bread, Milk : Item ;\n}\n\nconcrete ShopEng of Shop = {\n  lincat Phrase, Item = {s : Str} ;\n  lin Want x = {s = \"I want\" ++ x.s} ;\n      Bread = {s = \"bread\"} ;\n      Milk = {s = \"milk\"} ;\n}\n```\n\nA Spanish concrete syntax, `ShopSpa`, would use the same abstract syntax with `\"quiero\"` and `\"pan\"`/`\"leche\"`. Then, in the GF shell:\n\n```\n> parse -lang=ShopEng \"I want milk\" | linearize -lang=ShopSpa\nquiero leche\n```\n\n[WebFetch note: this page's text is 119305 characters long and the answer above covers only characters 0 to 100000; the final 19305 were not read — to read on, call WebFetch again with the same url and offset: 100000.]"

Key Technical Concepts:\n   - **Project.** `@link-foundation/universal-translator` v0.15.0 has matching JS (js/src) and Rust (rust/src) implementations that must produce byte-identical outputs. The lexer's `newline()` pushes nothing when there is no previous token, so blank lines at the start are dropped. `layout()` in meta/tree.js removes leading and trailing Blanks.\n   - **Lexer.** `space()` silently discards whitespace; tokens are `{type, value, line, ...}`. Comment tokens have `span` and `trailing` gap fields. Names are ASCII-only `[A-Za-z_]` (Unicode identifiers are needed for R8).\n   - **Emitter** (js/src/formal/emitter.js, 1072 lines) is line-based: `this.line(content)` pushes onto `this.lines`, and `statement(statement)` dispatches.\n     - `binary()` hardcodes `` `${left} ${operator} ${right}` ``.\n     - `Call` emits `` `${callee}(${args.join(', ')})` ``.\n     - Dialect emitters live in js/src/formal/dialects (ada, bash, fortran, lean, matlab, pascal, rocq, shared, vb, zig) and the same in rust/src/formal/dialects.\n   - **Requirements gate.** scripts/check-requirements.mjs reads `docs/case-studies/{issue-1,issue-6,issue-8}/requirements.lino`. Problem Solving (reproduced root-cause observations):\n   - **Whitespace.**\n     - Output is `print(\"Hello World!\")\\n\\nprint(1 + 2)\\n`: the leading blank line is lost (lexer and parser drop blanks before the first item; fragment `dedent` trims) and in-line spacing is lost (`space()` discards whitespace; the emitter hardcodes spaces).\n     - In fragment mode the blank line after a comment is lost too. The non-fragment path keeps it (`# Привет мир\\n\\nprint(...)`); the fragment path gives `# Привет мир\\nprint(...)`.\n   - **Comment translation.** `--comment-language english` leaves \"Привет мир\" unchanged because the dictionary has no such words.\n   - **Detection of «Привет».** `detect` outputs nothing.\n   - **«Как хорошо покакать?».** `detect` gives `(id minimal-russian) (natural true) (reads false) (coverage 0) (score 2)`. A base language should be preferred over its variants, and a fallback is needed for free text.\n   - **Planned design for R1 (generic trivia transfer).**\n     - The parser records a source line span on statement nodes.\n     - The emitter's `statement()` records the output line range of each statement, giving a source↔target statement map. This map is also reusable for the UI mapping, selection and scroll sync.\n     - A post-pass aligns tokens inside each mapped statement using a generic tokenizer that knows the target syntax's quotes and comment markers and never touches strings or comments. Alignment uses LCS on token values plus single-token substitutions such as `=`↔`:=`.\n     - The pass copies the source gaps onto the target gaps under safety rules: never touch indentation or newlines; never remove a space between word characters; remove a space between punctuation only when both tokens match exactly.\n     - Fragments re-attach the leading and trailing blank lines and the common indentation.\n     - The parser and lexer keep blank lines at program start.\n     - All of this must also be done in Rust, and the example outputs must stay consistent.\n   - **Planned for R9, R12–R14.**\n     - A concept-indexed multilingual dictionary data file (common words such as greetings, a Swadesh-style list) with parts of speech and inflected forms.\n     - Script- and dictionary-based detection of natural languages when nothing parses.\n     - Prefer base languages over variants.\n     - Word-by-word plus simple grammar translation between natural languages when no template matches.\n   - **Planned for R16:** generalize Print to a call to a standard-library function, at least in the meta view. The cost is large because Print is used across 32 emitters and lowering, in both JS and Rust.\n   - **Planned for R17:**\n     - new assembly dialects such as GAS AT&T and ARM64;\n     - new intermediate languages such as WebAssembly WAT and LLVM IR;\n     - make sure the UI lists the machine targets (nasm, cil, jvm already exist).\n\n6. translatated from C expression in `meta language` to equivalent expression  of C# `meta language` we can do materialization or formatting or translation from meta language to C#.\n\nIf `literal` accordingly.\n\n```\n/* Hello world in C */\n\n#include <stdio.h>\n\nmain()\n{\n    /* print \"Hello World!\" into console followed by new line symbol by function call */\n    printf(\"Hello World!\\n\");\n}\n```\n\ngoes to\n\n```\n/* Hello World in C# */\nclass HelloWorld\n{\n    static void Main()\n    {\n        /* print \"Hello World!\" into console followed by new line symbol by method call */\n        System.Console.WriteLine(\"Hello, World!\");\n    }\n}\n```\n\nFor example here we clearly updated the comment with C replaced to C#, `function call` -> `method call` and so on.\n\nSo by default we should use context dependent translation, with multiple configuration options like I described.\n\nOnce we finish with stabilization of translation between hello world programs, we should stabilize translation between all rosetta code examples.\n\nWe start by implementing our translator in JavaScript and Rust at the same time.\n\nWe should have just enough source Now `readStandardInput` waits through `EAGAIN`, and `EPIPE` ends the CLI quietly. You can paste a whole program, one function or one statement. The `web-e2e` job in `.github/workflows/example-app.yml` drives it in Chromium (`examples/universal-app/e2e/translate.e2e.mjs`) and takes the screenshot above.\n26-\n27-### Fragments: statements, functions or a whole program\n28-\n29-`translateFragment` / `parseFragment` (JS) and `translate_fragment` / `parse_fragment` (Rust), plus `universal-translator translate --fragment`, accept a statement, one or more functions, or a whole program. Each comes back as the same kind of fragment in the target. A fragment only has to be complete: a function must end with its closing. Otherwise the translator fails with the reason and the line, for example `The fragment is not complete: it ends before its closing (line 2)`. Goldens for every language are in `examples/programs/fragments/translated/` and are checked by `write-fragments.mjs --check`.\n30-\n31-### CLI, library, HTTP API and Docker\n32-\n33-- `universal-translator serve` starts an HTTP API (`GET /languages`, `POST /translate`). It reads `--port`/`--host`, then `PORT`/`HOST`, then `.lenv`, through lino-arguments.\n34-- `js/src/index.js` (with types) and the `rust/` crate are the libraries.\n35-- The `Dockerfile` image runs the CLI and the server. The release workflow builds it and smoke tests the CLI and the HTTP API.\n36-\n37-### Source layout and best practices\n38-\n39-- Sources are split into `src/meta` (shared types and trees), `src/formal` (programming languages, Lean, Rocq and machine code) and `src/natural` (human languages, with a reader and a writer), in both `js/` and `rust/`. The `source-layout` check rejects imports that point outwards from the meta layer.\n40-- [`docs/case-studies/issue-1/best-practices.md`](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-1-35d65b774bf6/docs/case-studies/issue-1/best-practices.md) maps the associative technology stack, the code architecture principles and all 17 CI/CD best practices to evidence, or gives a reason when one does not apply. `cargo clippy -D warnings` now runs in CI.\n41-- **Test coverage is required by CI.** `npm run test:coverage` replaces `npm test` in the Node.js job. It fails below 94% line, 91% branch or 95% function coverage of `js/src` and `bin`; current coverage is 95.4%, 92.1% and 96.5%. The Rust crate runs the same goldens, but CI does not measure its coverage.\n42-\n--\n96:**Blocked, with reasons recorded in `rosetta-coverage.lino`.** These are not presented as done.
