the two command lines print the same output                                              | the Rust tests named in each row                                                                 |\n\n### Status\n\nThis section is updated as the work lands. Rows R15, R16, R17, R20 and R23\nare in progress.\n\n## Root Causes\n\nEach problem was reproduced on `main` before the fix. The inputs are in\n`experiments/issue-14/`.\n\n1. **Whitespace is lost (screenshot 1).** The pipeline reads the source to a\n   meta program and prints the target from the meta program alone. The lexer\n   drops spaces, so the emitter can only print its own canonical spacing:\n\n   ```text\n   main:   console.log( \"Hello World!\");  ->  console.log(\"Hello World!\");\n   branch: console.log( \"Hello World!\");  ->  console.log( \"Hello World!\");\n   ```\n\n   This is the classic AST round-trip problem. Roslyn, rowan and LibCST solve\n   it with trivia attached to tokens. Their approach works when source and\n   target share one language and one token stream; a translation changes the\n   tokens. The layout pass (`layout.js`) therefore matches the tokens of the\n   output to those of the source, statement by statement. It then moves the\n   source's spacing, blank lines and comment placement onto the output. It\n   also returns a `lineMap` (output line to source line) that the web app\n   uses for the linked editors.\n\n2. **Comments are not translated (screenshot 2).** Two faults together:\n   - `detectCommentLanguage` scored languages only by the words of the\n     programming templates. «Привет мир» scored 0 everywhere, so it fell back\n     to `english`. With source and target both English, the comment stayed\n     the same.\n   - Even with `--comment-from russian`, the comment dictionary held only\n     the programming vocabulary of each language (`привет` and `мир` are not\n     in it), so no word was replaced:\n\n   ```text\n   main:   // Привет мир  --comment-language english  ->  // Привет мир\n   branch: // Привет мир  --comment-language english  ->  // Hello world\n   ```\n\n   Fix: a shared multilingual vocabulary (`data/natural/vocabulary.lino`,\n   concepts with words in every base language, ranked by frequency) feeds\n   both the detection and the translation of comments.\n\n3. **Auto-detection fails on «Привет» (screenshot 3).** `detectLanguage`\n   counted a natural-language word as evidence only when the language's\n   templates reserve it or its lexicon names it. A greeting is neither, and\n   no template reads it, so every natural language scored 0 and was filtered\n   out:\n\n   ```text\n   main:   detectLanguage('Привет')  ->  []\n   branch: detectLanguage('Привет')  ->  russian (natural) first, score 110\n   ```\n\n4. **«Как хорошо покакать?» fails to translate (screenshot 4).** A natural\n   source had to match a sentence template of an algorithm (`if ... then`,\n   `repeat ...`). Anything else failed with `No sentence template matches`.\n   The issue asks for free translation between natural languages, so a text\n   no template reads is now translated word by word and phrase by phrase\n   through the vocabulary:\n\n   ```text\n   main:   No sentence template matches\n   branch: Detected language: russian / How good to poop?\n   ```\n\n5. **Plain editor by default, no linked view.** The web app defaulted to a\n   textarea with highlight.js colours; Monaco was an option. The two editors\n   shared no state, so there was nothing to keep in sync and no line map to\n   show.\n\n6. **Comments are opaque strings in the meta language.** The meta program\n   kept comments and strings as plain text, so it could not express a code\n   fragment inside a comment or prose inside a string.\n\n7. **`print` is special in the meta language.** Each reader turned\n   `console.log`, `print`, `println!` and the others into a `Print` node, and\n   each emitter printed it. The meta language had no notion of a library\n   function. `meta/library.js` now generalizes such statements to\n   `Call print-line` and specializes them back for the target. The meta\n   notation shows the general form.\n\n## Solutions And Alternatives\n\n- **CST by default.** Alternatives considered (see `prior-art.md` section 1):\n  - a full lossless tree per language, Tree-sitter style. This needs a\n    second grammar for each of more than 30 languages, and does not help\n    across languages;\n  - trivia on meta nodes. This is lost when one statement becomes several.\n\n  The chosen layout pass works on token streams. It needs no grammar changes,\n  and when it cannot match a statement it falls back to the emitter's own\n  formatting.\n- **Linked editors.** Monaco's `onDidScrollChange`,\n  `onDidChangeCursorSelection` and the folding model keep the two editors\n  together through the `lineMap`. Scrolling is mapped block by block, so a\n  block of 3 lines that becomes 7 scrolls proportionally.\n- **Deeper natural language.** The GF approach (an abstract syntax of\n  concepts with one concrete grammar per language) matches the existing\n  meta-language design best. The vocabulary is the abstract lexicon. The\n  prose reader builds `Prose > Sentence > Word` with concept and part of\n  speech; Link Grammar and UD-style dependencies are the next layer\n  (`architecture.md`).\n- **Nested grammars.** These follow Tree-sitter injections: a node of one\n  grammar holds a reading in another. The reading sits next to the text, so\n  emitters that do not know it can ignore it, and `unnest` restores the plain\n  program.\n\n## Debug Output\n\n- `universal-translator translate ... --trace` (JavaScript and Rust) prints\n  the tree after each stage (`[parsed]`, `[understood]`, `[typed]`, the rule\n  layers) to standard error.\n- `universal-translator meta <language> <file>` prints the nested meta\n  program; `--shallow` prints the plain one, and `--json` prints it as JSON.\n- The web app logs editor, folding and mapping events to the console when\n  opened with `?debug` (`examples/universal-app/src/debug.js`).\n"
    }
  }

(b) JavaScript <->\n  Rust and JavaScript <-> Lean/Rocq with comments preserved; (c) grammar\n  definitions themselves (EBNF, ANTLR, Tree-sitter grammar JSON) as input for\n  new language tables; (d) the translation-rule files of\n  `docs/translation-rules.md` in that repository as **shared rule format**.\n  Recommendation: align node kinds, trivia names and the span model with\n  meta-language rather than inventing a second CST; contribute missing\n  features upstream.\n\n### 6.2 link-foundation/links-notation\n\n- What it is: \"A way to describe data using references and links.\"\n  Notation based on references and links with any number of references per\n  link (doublets, triplets, N-tuples, nesting by parentheses); hand-written\n  parsers in at least JavaScript, Rust, C#, Python, Go, Java, PHP, C++, Swift\n  and Kotlin, with a comparison against JSON and XML\n  ([README](https://github.com/link-foundation/links-notation)).\n- Translation cases: **Links Notation <-> JSON / YAML / XML**; links as the\n  serialization of CSTs and mapping records (section 4.2) so the UI and CLI\n  can export `--format lino`; natural-language statements such as\n  `papa has car` map directly to triplets, which is a ready-made target for\n  the NL abstract syntax in section 3.\n- Recommendation: use Links Notation as the **interchange format** for CST,\n  mapping table and lexicon entries; do not invent a new JSON schema.\n\n### 6.3 link-foundation/relative-meta-logic (RML)\n\n- What it is: a prototype logic framework \"that can reason about anything\n  relative to given probability of input statements\", formerly\n  \"Associative-Dependent Logic\". JavaScript and Rust implementations built on\n  Links Notation; many-valued and probabilistic logic with redefinable\n  operators, typed LiNo (`Pi`, `lambda`, `apply`, universes), a metatheorem\n  checker, an LSP server, and **exports to Lean 4, Rocq and Isabelle/HOL**\n  ([README](https://github.com/link-foundation/relative-meta-logic)).\n- Translation cases: (a) `.lino` typed fragment <-> Lean 4 and Rocq (the\n  translator already reads and writes both languages, so RML becomes a third\n  proof-language neighbour); (b) natural-language statements (\"probably\n  `A` implies `B`\") <-> RML expressions via the NL abstract syntax; (c) RML\n  source comments and truth annotations preserved (needs the CST rule).\n\n### 6.4 link-assistant/formal-ai\n\n- What it is: \"Don't know everything, know just enough to get to know\n  anything.\" A Rust implementation of a **symbolic, deterministic assistant**\n  exposing OpenAI-shaped APIs without neural inference; knowledge is a\n  readable semantic network in Links Notation; has a CLI, HTTP server,\n  Telegram bot, web demo via WebAssembly, Electron shell and VS Code\n  extension ([README](https://github.com/link-assistant/formal-ai),\n  [VISION.md](https://github.com/link-assistant/formal-ai/blob/main/VISION.md)).\n  VISION.md requires to \"preserve the complete readable CST, comments and\n  unrelated content, and verify JavaScript, TypeScript and Rust parity\", and\n  describes development performed through natural-language instructions.\n- Translation cases: **natural language -> code** and **code -> natural\n  language** (instructions such as \"rename X\" resolved against the CST),\n  JavaScript -> TypeScript -> Rust parity, and the Links Notation knowledge\n  base in several natural languages (which needs section 3).\n- Recommendation: treat formal-ai as the main consumer of the NL grammar:\n  a controlled natural-language instruction must parse to the same abstract\n  syntax the translator uses.\n\n### 6.5 link-assistant/router\n\n- What it is: a self-hosted gateway giving each task an expiring, revocable,\n  rate-limited token while keeping vendor credentials inside the router; a\n  transparent proxy for Anthropic and OpenAI-compatible APIs. It ships Rust,\n  JavaScript and Python packages and clients generated from OpenAPI. The\n  language layout document says native JavaScript lives in `js/src`, **TypeScript\n  is generated from JavaScript, Rust is the translated crate**, and the\n  forward and reverse commands (`scripts/translate-router.mjs`,\n  `scripts/regenerate-js-first.mjs`) must cross \"the checked, serialized and\n  reparsed CST/meta boundary\" with unknown constructs kept as explicit\n  refusals\n  ([README](https://github.com/link-assistant/router),\n  [language-layout.md](https://github.com/link-assistant/router/blob/main/docs/development/language-layout.md)).\n- Translation cases: **JavaScript -> TypeScript** (type annotations from type\n  inference), **JavaScript <-> Rust** for a real server codebase, repository\n  formatting and binding substitutions as a separate ordered rule layer,\n  configuration formats (OpenAPI YAML, JSON Schema, TOML manifests), and\n  generated clients in PHP, Go, Java. This is a large real-world regression\n  corpus for CST preservation: unchanged files must round trip, and unknown\n  constructs must fail loudly rather than being dropped.\n- Recommendation: use the router's JavaScript sources as a **soak test** in\n  CI (parse, print, compare bytes; translate to TypeScript and type check),\n  and copy its rule of \"explicit refusal for unknown constructs\".\n\n---\n\n## 7. Consolidated recommendations\n\nCST and whitespace\n\n1. Make the **lossless CST the default parse result**; derive the meta program\n   (AST view) from it with node ids and spans (rust-analyzer, meta-language\n   vision).\n2. Attach trivia with **Roslyn's rule** (trailing trivia to end of line, rest\n   leading on the next token); store byte spans and keep `print(parse(x)) === x`\n   as a repository-wide test on every example program and on router sources.\n3. Give comments and blank lines to the **following statement** (LibCST\n   `leading_lines`), store indent as depth plus a document indent unit, and\n   store comments as text plus a style so each emitter chooses delimiters.\n4. For same-language edits reuse original text for unchanged nodes (recast);\n   for cross-language output carry only trivia and pretty-print the rest.\n5. Never use a discarding parser stage without a side channel (Lark\n   `%ignore`, ANTLR `skip`): use hidden channels or Tree-sitter-style extras.\n\nNesting\n\n6. Colour nested regions with **CST-derived semantic tokens** rather than\n   Monarch.\n\nNatural language\n\n8. This is a large real-world regression\n  corpus for CST preservation: unchanged files must round trip, and unknown\n  constructs must fail loudly rather than being dropped.\n- Recommendation: use the router's JavaScript sources as a **soak test** in\n  CI (parse, print, compare bytes; translate to TypeScript and type check),\n  and copy its rule of \"explicit refusal for unknown constructs\".\n\n---\n\n## 7. Consolidated recommendations\n\nCST and whitespace\n\n1. Make the **lossless CST the default parse result**; derive the meta program\n   (AST view) from it with node ids and spans (rust-analyzer, meta-language\n   vision).\n2. Attach trivia with **Roslyn's rule** (trailing trivia to end of line, rest\n   leading on the next token); store byte spans and keep `print(parse(x)) === x`\n   as a repository-wide test on every example program and on router sources.\n3. Give comments and blank lines to the **following statement** (LibCST\n   `leading_lines`), store indent as depth plus a document indent unit, and\n   store comments as text plus a style so each emitter chooses delimiters.\n4. For same-language edits reuse original text for unchanged nodes (recast);\n   for cross-language output carry only trivia and pretty-print the rest.\n5. Never use a discarding parser stage without a side channel (Lark\n   `%ignore`, ANTLR `skip`): use hidden channels or Tree-sitter-style extras.\n\nNesting\n\n6. One mechanism: **`embedded(language, range, innerTree)` nodes created by\n   declarative injection rules** (Tree-sitter `injections.scm` semantics, with\n   `combined` for template literals), selected by node kind or call context,\n   separate from the 32 host grammars.\n7. Colour nested regions with **CST-derived semantic tokens** rather than\n   Monarch.\n\nNatural language\n\n8. Use **UD tags and CoNLL-U** for parts of speech, features and dependencies;\n   express agreement as **feature unification** (NLTK style).\n10. Word choice rule: concept match, then **round-trip filter**, then\n    **frequency rank**, then fewer senses; store as `preferred`.\n\nUI\n\n12.           "content": "# Architecture of the translator (issue 14)\n\nIssue 14 asks for an architecture that covers a wide range of cases without\nbeing rewritten later. It should:\n\n- keep a concrete syntax tree (CST) by default;\n- learn from ANTLR, Tree-sitter, Lark, spaCy, Stanza, NLTK, GF and Link\n  Grammar;\n- support the related projects: formal-ai, meta-language, router and\n  relative-meta-logic.\n\nThis document describes the layers as they are in the code and maps each one\nto those projects. It also states which cases each layer already handles and\nwhere new cases plug in. Sources for every external project are in\n`prior-art.md`.\n\n## The layers\n\n```text\n source text\n   │  reader (formal/lexer + table-driven parser, natural/reader)\n   ▼\n source tree ─── tokens with spans (the CST side channel)\n   │  understanding rules (formal/rules, lifting)\n   ▼\n meta program (meta/tree) ◄── nesting (translation/nesting): readings of\n   │                          comments and strings in their own grammars\n   │  standard library (meta/library): generalize print/length/... to calls\n   │  type inference (meta/types), meaning and context rules (mode)\n   │  comment and identifier languages (natural/comments,\n   │  translation/identifier-language)\n   ▼\n meta program for the target\n   │  specialize the library calls, lower (formal/lowering) for machine code\n   │  emitter (formal/emitter, natural/writer)\n   ▼\n target text\n   │  layout pass (translation/layout): source spacing, blank lines and\n   │  comment places moved onto the target; lineMap for the editors\n   ▼\n output + lineMap\n```\n\nEach arrow is a function with the same name and shape in both\nimplementations:\n\n- JavaScript: `js/src/translator.js` (`createGrammarTranslator`);\n- Rust: `rust/src/translator.rs` (`Translator`).\n\nThe meta language depends on no language family, and natural languages do\nnot depend on formal ones. The `source-layout` check of\n`scripts/check-requirements.mjs` enforces this.\n\n### Why the CST is a token side channel\n\n`prior-art.md` section 1 compares two ways to keep every character:\n\n- full lossless trees (Roslyn, rowan, swift-syntax, Tree-sitter);\n- trivia attached to tokens (LibCST, recast).\n\nBoth are built for one language. A translation replaces the tokens, so trivia\nattached to source tokens has nowhere to go in the target. The translator\ntherefore keeps two views:\n\n- the **lossless view**: the token stream with byte spans, including spaces\n  and comments. A source document (`translation/source-document.js`, built on\n  `meta-language`'s `LinkType`) prints back byte for byte;\n- the **meaning view**: the meta program. It is an AST, but every node can be\n  traced back to tokens, and the layout pass uses that trace to carry the\n  source's layout to the target.\n\nThe lossless view is the default everywhere:\n\n- `--layout source` is the default in both command lines and the server;\n- the web app keeps the layout;\n- comment translation in place (`translateComments`) changes only the words\n  inside comments.\n\nThe canonical target layout is an option: `--layout target`.\n\nThis matches the meta-language vision: \"complete concrete syntax trees,\nproduced by default\", with an AST that has provenance back to the CST.\n\n### Nested grammars\n\nThis follows Tree-sitter injections (`prior-art.md` section 2). A node of one\ngrammar keeps its text and gains a `reading` in another grammar:\n\n| Host        | Nested reading                   | Example                                  |\n| ----------- | -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |\n| comment     | `Prose > Sentence > Word`        | `// Prints the sum`                      |\n| prose       | `Code` (any programming language) | `` // Prints `x + 1` ``                  |\n| string      | `Code` when it reads as code     | `code = \"print(1 + 2)\"`                  |\n| string      | `Prose` otherwise                | `\"Привет мир\"`                           |\n| long texts  | `Paragraph` under `texts`, by id | a comment and a string with the same text |\n\nReadings are additions. An emitter that does not know them ignores them, and\n`unnest` returns the plain program. New host or nested languages therefore\nneed no change to the emitters. A new grammar becomes nestable as soon as\n`parseFragment` reads it.\n\n### Natural language\n\nThe design follows GF (`prior-art.md` section 3.1):\n\n- **abstract syntax**: concepts. Words in `data/natural/vocabulary.lino` and\n  sentence templates in `data/natural/<language>.lino` are keyed by concept\n  ids such as `hello`, `print` and `if`;\n- **concrete syntax**: one description per language. Templates read and\n  write whole algorithm sentences. The prose reader\n  (`natural/prose-reading`) reads any other text into words, each with its\n  concept and part of speech;\n- **lexical choice**: the first word of a concept is the most frequent one.\n  Translation picks it unless the source used a word that survives the round\n  trip (`prior-art.md` section 3.9).\n\nNew depth is added in the same tree, so nothing is rewritten:\n\n- morphology (UniMorph features) goes on `Word`;\n- dependencies (Universal Dependencies or Link Grammar links) are links\n  between the `Word`s of a `Sentence`.\n\nThe spaCy, Stanza and NLTK pipelines (tokenize, tag, parse) correspond to the\nreader stages. We do not use them at run time: their models are large and\nwritten in Python, and the translator must run in a browser.\n\n### Targets beyond source languages\n\nMachine targets (NASM, CIL, JVM) use the same meta program, lowered first\n(`formal/lowering`). They can be read back (`formal/machine-reader`, lifting).\nAssembly dialects and other intermediate languages are a syntax table over a\nshared instruction model, as `prior-art.md` section 5.3 recommends.       "content": "# Architecture of the translator (issue 14)\n\nIssue 14 asks for an architecture that covers a wide range of cases without\nbeing rewritten later. It should:\n\n- keep a concrete syntax tree (CST) by default;\n- learn from ANTLR, Tree-sitter, Lark, spaCy, Stanza, NLTK, GF and Link\n  Grammar;\n- support the related projects: formal-ai, meta-language, router and\n  relative-meta-logic.\n\nThis document describes the layers as they are in the code and maps each one\nto those projects. It also states which cases each layer already handles and\nwhere new cases plug in. Sources for every external project are in\n`prior-art.md`.\n\n## The layers\n\n```text\n source text\n   │  reader (formal/lexer + table-driven parser, natural/reader)\n   ▼\n source tree ─── tokens with spans (the CST side channel)\n   │  understanding rules (formal/rules, lifting)\n   ▼\n meta program (meta/tree) ◄── nesting (translation/nesting): readings of\n   │                          comments and strings in their own grammars\n   │  standard library (meta/library): generalize print/length/... to calls\n   │  type inference (meta/types), meaning and context rules (mode)\n   │  comment and identifier languages (natural/comments,\n   │  translation/identifier-language)\n   ▼\n meta program for the target\n   │  specialize the library calls, lower (formal/lowering) for machine code\n   │  emitter (formal/emitter, natural/writer)\n   ▼\n target text\n   │  layout pass (translation/layout): source spacing, blank lines and\n   │  comment places moved onto the target; lineMap for the editors\n   ▼\n output + lineMap\n```\n\nEach arrow is a function with the same name and shape in both\nimplementations:\n\n- JavaScript: `js/src/translator.js` (`createGrammarTranslator`);\n- Rust: `rust/src/translator.rs` (`Translator`).\n\nThe meta language depends on no language family, and natural languages do\nnot depend on formal ones. The `source-layout` check of\n`scripts/check-requirements.mjs` enforces this.\n\n### Why the CST is a token side channel\n\n`prior-art.md` section 1 compares two ways to keep every character:\n\n- full lossless trees (Roslyn, rowan, swift-syntax, Tree-sitter);\n- trivia attached to tokens (LibCST, recast).\n\nBoth are built for one language. A translation replaces the tokens, so trivia\nattached to source tokens has nowhere to go in the target. The translator\ntherefore keeps two views:\n\n- the **lossless view**: the token stream with byte spans, including spaces\n  and comments. A source document (`translation/source-document.js`, built on\n  `meta-language`'s `LinkType`) prints back byte for byte;\n- the **meaning view**: the meta program. It is an AST, but every node can be\n  traced back to tokens, and the layout pass uses that trace to carry the\n  source's layout to the target.\n\nThe lossless view is the default everywhere:\n\n- `--layout source` is the default in both command lines and the server;\n- the web app keeps the layout;\n- comment translation in place (`translateComments`) changes only the words\n  inside comments.\n\nThe canonical target layout is an option: `--layout target`.\n\nThis matches the meta-language vision: \"complete concrete syntax trees,\nproduced by default\", with an AST that has provenance back to the CST.\n\n### Nested grammars\n\nThis follows Tree-sitter injections (`prior-art.md` section 2). A node of one\ngrammar keeps its text and gains a `reading` in another grammar:\n\n| Host        | Nested reading                   | Example                                  |\n| ----------- | -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |\n| comment     | `Prose > Sentence > Word`        | `// Prints the sum`                      |\n| prose       | `Code` (any programming language) | `` // Prints `x + 1` ``                  |\n| string      | `Code` when it reads as code     | `code = \"print(1 + 2)\"`                  |\n| string      | `Prose` otherwise                | `\"Привет мир\"`                           |\n| long texts  | `Paragraph` under `texts`, by id | a comment and a string with the same text |\n\nReadings are additions. An emitter that does not know them ignores them, and\n`unnest` returns the plain program. New host or nested languages therefore\nneed no change to the emitters. A new grammar becomes nestable as soon as\n`parseFragment` reads it.\n\n### Natural language\n\nThe design follows GF (`prior-art.md` section 3.1):\n\n- **abstract syntax**: concepts. Words in `data/natural/vocabulary.lino` and\n  sentence templates in `data/natural/<language>.lino` are keyed by concept\n  ids such as `hello`, `print` and `if`;\n- **concrete syntax**: one description per language. Templates read and\n  write whole algorithm sentences. The prose reader\n  (`natural/prose-reading`) reads any other text into words, each with its\n  concept and part of speech;\n- **lexical choice**: the first word of a concept is the most frequent one.\n  Translation picks it unless the source used a word that survives the round\n  trip (`prior-art.md` section 3.9).\n\nNew depth is added in the same tree, so nothing is rewritten:\n\n- morphology (UniMorph features) goes on `Word`;\n- dependencies (Universal Dependencies or Link Grammar links) are links\n  between the `Word`s of a `Sentence`.\n\nThe spaCy, Stanza and NLTK pipelines (tokenize, tag, parse) correspond to the\nreader stages. We do not use them at run time: their models are large and\nwritten in Python, and the translator must run in a browser.\n\n### Targets beyond source languages\n\nMachine targets (NASM, CIL, JVM) use the same meta program, lowered first\n(`formal/lowering`). They can be read back (`formal/machine-reader`, lifting).\nAssembly dialects and other intermediate languages are a syntax table over a\nshared instruction model, as `prior-art.md` section 5.3 recommends. A new\ndialect is a new table, not a new pipeline.\n\n## The related projects\n\n| Project                               | What it needs from the translator                                                                       | Where it plugs in                                                                                                                                                    |\n| ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| link-foundation/meta-language         | a CST by default, an AST with provenance, every language, Links Notation as the format                  | the source document already uses `meta-language`; `meta` prints the meta program as Links Notation (`meta/notation`); node kinds keep the meta-language names        |\n| link-foundation/links-notation        | one interchange format                                                                                  | every data file (`data/**/*.lino`), the meta notation, the requirements lists and `--rules` files are Links Notation                                                  |\n| link-foundation/relative-meta-logic   | translation between its typed Links Notation fragments, Lean 4 and Rocq; statements in natural language | Lean and Rocq are readers and emitters already; truth values are in `meta/truth`; natural statements go through the prose reader                                     |\n| link-assistant/formal-ai              | natural-language instructions to code and back; comments and unrelated content kept                     | natural ↔ formal translation through the shared concepts; the CST default keeps comments; the library and the HTTP server (`serve`) are the integration points |\n| link-assistant/router                 | JavaScript → TypeScript and JavaScript ↔ Rust for a real code base; unknown constructs refused loudly   | partial translation marks every part it cannot read (`translatePartial`), and `--all-or-nothing` refuses; the layout pass keeps formatting                           |\n\nThe table also shows how the architecture extends to these cases. A standard starts from the semantic primes of its language and the\n//! grammatical words its minimal profile allows. Every other word is a\n//! composite word with a definition made only of words the standard already\n//! has, so every word expands down to the primes. A standard holds at most\n//! [`STANDARD_WORD_LIMIT`] words.\n//!\n//! [`define_word`] extends a standard: it looks up the definition of an\n//! unknown word, defines every unknown word of that definition the same way,\n//! recursively, and adds the word when its definition is made only of words\n//! of the standard.\n//!\n//! # The Wikidata definitions\n//!\n//! The JavaScript `wikidataLookup` fetches the glosses of Wikidata lexemes\n//! over HTTPS and keeps every answer in a cache file\n//! (`data/definitions/wikidata-<language>.lino`, written by\n//! `scripts/precache-definitions.mjs`). The Rust standard library has no\n//! HTTPS client, so Rust never fetches: [`wikidata_lookup`] answers from a\n//! [`DefinitionCache`] read from the very file format the JavaScript side\n//! writes ([`read_definition_cache`] and [`write_definition_cache`] are the\n//! twins of `readDefinitionCache` and `writeDefinitionCache`). A word that is\n//! not in the cache has no definitions, as an empty lookup does in\n//! JavaScript. [`precached_definitions`] is the cache shipped with the crate.\n//! self.primitives.iter().any(|(known, _)| known == word)\n    }\n\n    pub fn has_definition(&self, word: &str) -> bool {\n        self.definitions.iter().any(|(known, _)| known == word)\n    }\n\n Key Technical Concepts:\n   - **JS ↔ Rust parity:** Rust Node fields are a BTreeMap (sorted); JS keeps insertion order. The two CLIs must give identical output.\n   - **Layout pass** (layout.js and layout.rs): a CST token side channel.\n     - Both texts are cut into tokens and aligned (common prefix and suffix, unique-token anchors, LCS).\n     - Aligned neighbours take the source's spaces.\n     - The outer blank lines are kept.\n     - Indentation and line breaks stay as the target writes them.\n     - It returns a lineMap.\n     - `--layout source|target`, source is the default.\n   - **Nesting:** nestGrammars and unnest.\n     - Readings: Prose > Sentence > Word, Code, and Paragraph texts with id `text-N` for texts over 12 words.\n     - `meta` nests unless `--shallow`.\n   - **Standard library:** generalize/specialize, so print becomes `Call print-line`.\n   - **Editor sync** (editor-sync.js) listens to:\n     - onDidChangeCursorSelection;\n     - onDidScrollChange;\n     - onDidChangeHiddenAreas;\n     - onDidChangeModelContent;\n     - onDidLayoutChange;\n     - onDidContentSizeChange.\n\n     mapping.js colours line groups and draws an SVG strip between the editors. `?debug` or localStorage turns on debug logging.\n   - **Web build:**\n     - chunk-limits.js keeps every non-Monaco chunk at or under 500 kB;\n     - the natural data is split into the natural-vocabulary chunk.\n   - **Requirements gate:** scripts/check-requirements.mjs.\n     - caseStudies is `['issue-1','issue-6','issue-8']` at line 17.\n     - It reads `requirements.lino` entries of the form:\n       ```\n       requirements:\n         id:\n           text: '...'\n           from: '...'\n           status: done|blocked\n           evidence: paths\n           check: name\n           reason: '...'\n       ```\n     - Any status other than done or blocked fails CI. `--strict` also fails blocked entries.\n   - **Natural templates** in data/natural/<lang>.lino: the first template is the one written; the other variants are only read.\n\n3. Key Technical Concepts:\n   - The pipeline stages are parse, infer, lift, readMachine, readNatural, emit, emitMachineCode and writeNatural. Decorators wrap each stage; the first listed is innermost and the last is outermost.\n   - JS `createGrammarTranslator` (exported as `createTranslator`) uses `buildStages(settings)`, which applies `decorateStages`. Rust uses a `Stages` struct of `Arc<dyn Fn>` stage types (rust/src/stages.rs) and `Translator::decorate_*` methods.\n   - Language versions are written `id@version`. A version changes writing only; reading accepts all versions. In JS, version syntax is merged into the language syntax by `mergeSyntax` (nested records are merged, other values replaced). In Rust, `Syntax` is a typed struct and versions are `fn(&mut Syntax)` in the static `LANGUAGE_VERSIONS` table, with `with_version`.\n   - The emitter is table-driven by `this.id`, with syntax flags such as `textJoin`, `integerDivision` ({wrapper|call|method}), `textConversions`, `arrayFill`, `declarations` and `version`.\n   - The context rules adapt to the base language id. `expandArrayFills` now needs the versioned target. JS passes `settings.target`; Rust still needs a `Settings.target` field.\n   - Genuine version differences chosen:\n     - es5: `var`, `+` concatenation with `String()`, `~~(a / b)` truncation, `new Array(n)` plus a fill loop.\n     - php5: `(int) (a / b)` instead of `intdiv`, and `array(...)` literals.\n     - csharp5: `+` concatenation with `System.Convert.ToString`, with no `$\"\"`.\n     - Optional and heavy: cpp98 (a `to_string` helper, no vector initializer list) and c89 (declaration hoisting, no stdbool).\n   - Environment: the cgroup memory limit is about 3.1 GB, shared among agents, so rustc gets OOM-killed. Fix: copy a built target dir from another worktree. Tools available: node 26, php, gcc/g++, javac, dotnet. ESLint and Prettier live at ../../../node_modules/.bin. helloworldcollection.de is served over GitHub Pages: http works, https needs `curl -k`.\n\n3. It is a regex on the meaning id.\n- **Wrong accusative on intransitive verbs:** the accusative applies after any verb concept, so an intransitive verb followed by a noun ending in -а or -я is wrongly inflected.
